title: Get rich quick schema
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien uses semantic network theory and schemas to explain how expertise forms and why it can go wrong. He opens with personal examples of memories bound together, then defines a schema as a connected map of ideas that lets teachers make the 1,200 to 1,500 micro-decisions a day almost automatically. The twist, prompted by Sachdeva and Kirschner's Becoming an Expert Teacher, is that schemas are not always positive: online echo chambers can harden beliefs in productive struggle or pure inquiry, and a teacher who learns that shouting and exiting a student calms the room reinforces a schema that blocks growth. He connects this to Ausubel's meaningful learning, to the case for explicit instruction built on connected rather than isolated facts, and to the use of Do Nows to activate prior knowledge. His practical advice is to read widely, including sources that challenge one's beliefs, so schemas keep being tested.
points: Schemas let experts act on heuristics without conscious thought, but the same mechanism entrenches weak habits, such as a teacher who always removes disruptive students.
Echo-chamber algorithms can strengthen schemas in pedagogical beliefs through confirmation bias, so teachers should deliberately read sources that conflict with their view.
Teacher improvement plateaus after about five years unless existing schemas are challenged, which means 'what works' is not necessarily what is best.
Facts only support transfer when students understand the words and ideas inside them, so explicit instruction should build connected networks rather than isolated facts.
A Do Now does more than fight forgetting: it activates the prior knowledge that new learning needs to attach to.
quotes: A schema is a mental framework or map of connected ideas. These connections allow us to quickly leap between related concepts and problem solve based on ideas that our previous experiences tell us could apply to the situation.

If you have ever observed a truly expert teacher it may seem like they have a sixth sense, almost as if they are seeing the future before it happens and making adjustments to ensure that the ideal outcome happens.

In recently reading ‘Becoming an Expert Teacher’ by Nidhi Sachdeva and Paul Kirschner however I had an alarming thought. What if schemas are not always positive? I started spiralling a little bit thinking of the online educational discourse and the way our algorithms are set up to create an echo chamber for us which satisfies our confirmation bias.

A teacher may develop a schema that if a class is disruptive that yelling at and exiting a student leads the rest of the class to be calm. In that teacher’s mind there is now an A to B logic that if I shout and send them out then teaching will be more effective. Every time that scenario plays out it creates a stronger schema and therefore heuristic for the teacher to follow which may mean that they may never develop the expertise to best help the students in front of them.

On average teachers improve regardless of other factors for the first five years of their career and then plateau for the next two decades before having a slight decline. This tells me that unless schemas are continued to be challenged and built on after those first five years then teachers are likely to ‘do what works’ but what works isn’t necessarily what is best.

Don’t get me wrong, we definitely want students to be memorising key facts, however those facts are useless unless they know what the ideas and words within those facts mean. A student may memorise the definition that ‘inertia’ means an object resisting change in its state of motion but within that if the student doesn’t understand the word ‘resisting’ or ‘state of motion’ then they’ll be unable to apply their knowledge in new and novel contexts.

This also highlights the importance of activating prior knowledge in our lessons. A ‘Do Now’ activity may seem as if it is solely to fight forgetting by having students retrieve key information as a form of practice, but it also aims to activate the relevant knowledge to connect the new learning to. This means that students do not create isolated islands of knowledge and instead create a rich network of understanding.
For our students, building schemas mean that a single word in an exam question can suddenly light up an entire roadmap in their brain and allow them to express their knowledge fluently and in depth.
